node.label: Canadian women's & gender history
node.period_rationale: Selected Canadian milestones cluster from 1976 (collections, Strong-Boag) through the 1980s syntheses, i.e. 'Reorientations, c. 1970–85', with the gender-history debate in period_3. Cleverdon (1950) is an earlier witness, not an origin. Matches groups.json (period_2/period_3).
node.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1950 is an earlier witness; 1982 and 1988 are syntheses, not foundings; 1995–96 dates a debate, not an end. Post-2000 works sit in extension_coverage.

node.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
node.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in quebec_historiography, where 91% of its citing PhDs sit; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to quebec_historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) have primary placements in native_newcomer and settler_colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with moral_regulation; childhood and family with cdn_childhood_youth. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in cdn_working_class, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Cook and Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976); Strong-Boag, The Parliament of Women (1976); Kealey, ed., A Not Unreasonable Claim (1979). Collectif Clio, L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982; Quebec Women, 1987); Prentice et al., Canadian Women: A History (1988). Pierson, "They're Still Women After All" (1986); Danylewycz, Taking the Veil (1987); Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled (1988); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). Comparison: Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" (1980); Perry, On the Edge of Empire (2001). Extension: Fahrni (2005), Campbell (2009), Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018), Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023).

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (extension).
strands.works: Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Prentice, “Laying Siege to the History Professoriate” (1997); Cleverdon (1950); Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018)

strands.title: Suffrage, reform and early collections
strands.focus: Earlier work on suffrage and 1970s collections on women's place, organizations and reform. Earlier witnesses, not a single origin.
strands.works: Catherine L. Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1950).; Ramsay Cook and Wendy Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere: Woman's Place in Canadian Society (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1976).; Veronica Strong-Boag, The Parliament of Women: The National Council of Women of Canada, 1893–1929 (Ottawa, 1976; JSTOR edition published by the Canadian Museum of History).; Linda Kealey, ed., A Not Unreasonable Claim: Women and Reform in Canada, 1880s–1920s (Toronto: Women's Press, 1979).

strands.title: National syntheses
strands.focus: The collaborative English-language survey (1988) read against the Collectif Clio’s Quebec synthesis (1982; English 1987), whose main treatment is now in quebec_historiography (Q38).
strands.works: Collectif Clio (Micheline Dumont, Michèle Jean, Marie Lavigne and Jennifer Stoddart), L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (Montréal: Quinze, 1982).; Clio Collective, Quebec Women: A History (Toronto: Women's Press, 1987).; Alison Prentice, Paula Bourne, Gail Cuthbert Brandt, Beth Light, Wendy Mitchinson and Naomi Black, Canadian Women: A History (Toronto: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1988).

strands.title: Work, family, war and the state
strands.focus: Women's waged and unpaid work, family economies, the left, war and welfare; links to labour and family history.
strands.works: Ruth Roach Pierson, "They're Still Women After All": The Second World War and Canadian Womanhood (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1986).; Veronica Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled: Lives of Girls and Women in English Canada, 1919–1939 (Toronto: Copp Clark Pitman, 1988).; Joan Sangster, Dreams of Equality: Women on the Canadian Left, 1920–1950 (Toronto, 1989).; Joy Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners: Women, Men, and Change in Two Industrial Towns, 1880–1950 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1990).; Denyse Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (Montréal: Éditions du Remue-ménage, 1991).; Bettina Bradbury, Working Families: Age, Gender, and Daily Survival in Industrializing Montreal (Toronto, 1993).; Nancy Christie, Engendering the State: Family, Work, and Welfare in Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2000).; Lara Campbell, Respectable Citizens: Gender, Family, and Unemployment in Ontario's Great Depression (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2009).

strands.title: Bodies, sexuality and the law
strands.focus: Medicine, sexual violence and norms of female conduct; overlaps moral_regulation, where the regulatory framing is developed.
strands.works: Andrée Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes: des femmes au Québec pendant l'entre-deux-guerres (Montréal: Éditions du Remue-ménage, 1989).; Wendy Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies: Women and Their Doctors in Victorian Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1991).; Franca Iacovetta and Mariana Valverde, eds., Gender Conflicts: New Essays in Women's History (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992).; Karen Dubinsky, Improper Advances: Rape and Heterosexual Conflict in Ontario, 1880–1929 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993).

strands.title: Gender history and women's history: the dichotomies exchange
strands.focus: Whether gender history extends or displaces women’s history. Pierson’s 1991 essay opens on the turn to deconstruction and Scott. Sangster’s “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995), by her own later account, protested “the hierarchy being established between a superior gender history and a ‘limited’ women’s history”; replies by Dubinsky and Marks and by Iacovetta and Kealey defended gender history against her dichotomy, and she answered (1996). She later found the exchange “not very satisfying, with discussants sometimes talking at cross-purposes”. The replies were not read; their positions are not characterised further.
strands.works: Ruth Roach Pierson, "Experience, Difference, Dominance and Voice in the Writing of Canadian Women's History," in Writing Women's History, ed. Karen Offen, Ruth Roach Pierson and Jane Rendall (Basingstoke: Macmillan, 1991), 79–106.; Joy Parr, "Gender History and Historical Practice," Canadian Historical Review 76, no. 3 (1995): 354–376.; Joan Sangster, "Beyond Dichotomies: Re-Assessing Gender History and Women's History in Canada," Left History 3, no. 1 (Spring/Summer 1995): 109–21.; Karen Dubinsky and Lynne Marks, "Beyond Purity: A Response to Sangster," Left History 3, no. 2, and 4, no. 1 (Fall 1996): 205–20.; Franca Iacovetta and Linda Kealey, "Women's History, Gender History and Debating Dichotomies," Left History 3, no. 2, and 4, no. 1 (Fall 1996): 221–37.; Joan Sangster, "Reconsidering Dichotomies," Left History 3, no. 2, and 4, no. 1 (Fall 1996): 239–48.; Joan Sangster, Through Feminist Eyes (2011), introduction.

strands.title: Masculinity and gendered political languages
strands.focus: Gender as a relation in politics, religion and masculinity.
strands.works: Cecilia Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women: The Gendered Languages of Religion and Politics in Upper Canada, 1791–1850 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1996).; Kathryn McPherson, Cecilia Morgan and Nancy M. Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts: Historical Essays in Femininity and Masculinity in Canada (1999; University of Toronto Press reprint, 2003).

strands.title: Postwar domesticity and consumption
strands.focus: Domestic goods, women's magazines and household politics after 1945.
strands.works: Joy Parr, Domestic Goods: The Material, the Moral, and the Economic in the Postwar Years (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1999).; Valerie J. Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs: Reading Chatelaine Magazine in the Fifties and Sixties (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2000).; Magda Fahrni, Household Politics: Montreal Families and Postwar Reconstruction (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2005).

strands.title: Women religious in Quebec, and the critique of Quebec historiography
strands.focus: Danylewycz on taking the veil as an alternative to marriage and motherhood. The Collectif Clio and Lévesque’s critique of a male-centred Quebec history is kept here only as the basis of the critique edge cwg_rel_03; the Quebec women’s history strand (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) is primary in quebec_historiography (Q38).
strands.works: Marta Danylewycz, Taking the Veil: An Alternative to Marriage, Motherhood, and Spinsterhood in Quebec, 1840–1920 (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1987).; Collectif Clio (Micheline Dumont, Michèle Jean, Marie Lavigne and Jennifer Stoddart), L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (Montréal: Quinze, 1982).; Andrée Lévesque, "Réflexions sur l'histoire des femmes dans l'histoire du Québec," Revue d'histoire de l'Amérique française 51, no. 2 (1997): 271–284.

strands.title: Comparisons: fur-trade women and gender on the edge of empire
strands.focus: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Perry’s gender and race in colonial British Columbia (2001) are among the works most cited by this field’s PhDs but have primary placements in native_newcomer and settler_colonialism (Q39).

proposed_relationships.relationship: National and Quebec syntheses of women's history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The atlas's women entry groups national and regional syntheses (French, German, Nigerian) in a strand with different scopes and documentary bases. The Collectif Clio's Quebec synthesis (1982), which rejects a male-centred collective history, and Prentice et al.'s survey (1988) can be read alongside them. Comparison, not descent: Canadian women's history is not presented as a branch of any one national model.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Canadian debates over gender as a category
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Pierson's 1991 essay opens on feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis, naming Scott's theory of gender as the most acclaimed example. Parr (1995) and the 1995–96 Left History exchange (Sangster; Iacovetta and Kealey; Dubinsky and Marks) argued over gender history and women's history; their citations are checked, and Sangster's own position is taken from her 2011 retrospect; the replies are read only as defences of gender history. PhD context: 64 of 328 PhDs engaging this group cite Scott (20% vs 9% of all; lift 2.12).

proposed_relationships.relationship: Women's history questions a male-centred Quebec history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The Collectif Clio's introduction argues that a history centred on male figures had been presented as the collective history of the whole population. Lévesque's 1997 assessment says women's history redefined traditional Quebec history and hopes the slowness of some colleagues to integrate women is a matter of time and generation. A specific critique of how Quebec historiography treated women, not a rejection of that historiography. Coexists with qcreq_rel_07 (comparison) in drafts/quebec_historiography: a broad comparison and this specific critique can stand together, as GRAPH-FORMAT.md allows. Kept after Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) was made primary in quebec_historiography (Q38).

proposed_relationships.relationship: Gender as a dimension of class and family economies
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Parr's comparison of a textile town where most wage earners were women with a furniture town challenges conventional views of the distinctiveness of gender and class roles (author's book page). Bradbury's Working Families (age, gender and family survival) and Sangster's Dreams of Equality (women on the left) are title-level. Contribution of gender analysis to labour history; it does not claim the new labour history lacked it entirely. PhD context: 130 of 287 2009–2026 PhDs engaging cdn_women_gender also engage cdn_working_class (45%; lift 2.81), counted after removing shared anchors (Bradbury, Parr, Sangster). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Postwar domestic goods, magazines and households
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Parr's Domestic Goods (1999), Korinek's reading of Chatelaine (2000) and Fahrni's Household Politics (2005) place women and households at the centre of postwar consumption. Title-level only: none of these books was read, so the comparison is a teaching pointer to the consumption entry, not a claim about their arguments.

open_questions: Label: keep 'women's & gender history' as one entry, or split women's history and gender history? The 1995–96 exchange argues about exactly this; one entry with a debate strand is proposed.
The Left History texts (Sangster 1995, 1996; Iacovetta and Kealey 1996; Dubinsky and Marks 1996) could not be read (bot check). Should someone read them before the strand characterises positions?
Is Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) a fair 'critic' here? It is cited by title only; it may belong only in cdn_working_class.
